theory.intro: Two rectangles can have the **same area** but **different perimeters**. A long, thin rectangle has a larger perimeter than a more square one of equal area. To find all the rectangles with whole-number side lengths, list pairs that multiply to the area. A turned rectangle is counted only once.
facts: Check every whole-number pair without counting a turned rectangle twice. For a required perimeter, compare the perimeter of each pair.
steps: Find or list the rectangle dimensions and check the area.
Compare the results or check the required condition.

workedExamples.question_text: Rectangle A measures $22\text{ cm}$ by $3\text{ cm}$. Rectangle B measures $11\text{ cm}$ by $6\text{ cm}$. Show that their areas are equal, then find which has the smaller perimeter and by how much.
workedExamples.solution_text:
**Find or list the rectangle dimensions and check the area.**
A and B use different pairs of lengths.

**Find the perimeters when needed.**
$22\times3=66\text{ cm}^2$.
$11\times6=66\text{ cm}^2$.
$P_A=2\times(22+3)=50\text{ cm}$.
$P_B=2\times(11+6)=34\text{ cm}$.
$50-34=16\text{ cm}$.

**Compare the results or check the required condition.**
Their areas are equal. B has the smaller perimeter by $16\text{ cm}$.

workedExamples.question_text:
(a) List every different rectangle with whole-number side lengths and area $42\text{ cm}^2$. Give each perimeter, counting a turned rectangle only once.
(b) Find the smallest perimeter and the difference between the greatest and smallest perimeters.
workedExamples.solution_text:
**Find or list the rectangle dimensions and check the area.**
(a) List the whole-number pairs for $42$.

**Find the perimeters when needed.**
$1\times42$: $P=86\text{ cm}$.
$2\times21$: $P=46\text{ cm}$.
$3\times14$: $P=34\text{ cm}$.
$6\times7$: $P=26\text{ cm}$.
(b) $86-26=60\text{ cm}$.

**Compare the results or check the required condition.**
(a) There are $4$ rectangles. (b) The smallest perimeter is $26\text{ cm}$ for $6\text{ cm}$ by $7\text{ cm}$. The difference is $60\text{ cm}$.

workedExamples.question_text:
Rectangle A has area $70\text{ m}^2$ and length $14\text{ m}$. Rectangle B measures $10\text{ m}$ by $7\text{ m}$.
(a) Find A's width.
(b) Compare the perimeters.
workedExamples.solution_text:
**Find or list the rectangle dimensions and check the area.**
(a) Area $=$ length $\times$ width. Divide the area by the given length.

**Find the perimeters when needed.**
(a) $70\div14=5\text{ m}$.
(b) $P_A=2\times(14+5)=38\text{ m}$.
$P_B=2\times(10+7)=34\text{ m}$.
$38-34=4\text{ m}$.

**Compare the results or check the required condition.**
(a) A's width is $5\text{ m}$. (b) B has the smaller perimeter by $4\text{ m}$.

workedExamples.question_text:

(b) How many different whole-number rectangles have area $90\text{ m}^2$ and perimeter at most $44\text{ m}$? Give their dimensions.
workedExamples.solution_text:
**Find or list the rectangle dimensions and check the area.**
List whole-number pairs and check each required perimeter.

**Find the perimeters when needed.**
(a) $1\times84$: $P=170\text{ cm}$.
$2\times42$: $P=88\text{ cm}$.
$3\times28$: $P=62\text{ cm}$.
$4\times21$: $P=50\text{ cm}$.
$6\times14$: $P=40\text{ cm}$.
$7\times12$: $P=38\text{ cm}$.
(b) $1\times90$: $P=182\text{ m}$.
$2\times45$: $P=94\text{ m}$.
$3\times30$: $P=66\text{ m}$.
$5\times18$: $P=46\text{ m}$.
$6\times15$: $P=42\text{ m}$.
$9\times10$: $P=38\text{ m}$.

**Compare the results or check the required condition.**
(a) $6\text{ cm}$ by $14\text{ cm}$. (b) $2$ rectangles: $6\text{ m}$ by $15\text{ m}$ and $9\text{ m}$ by $10\text{ m}$.

foundation.question_text:
Rectangles with dimensions $1\text{ cm}\times16\text{ cm}$, $2\text{ cm}\times8\text{ cm}$ and $4\text{ cm}\times4\text{ cm}$ all have the same area.
Order them from smallest to largest perimeter.
foundation.solution_text:
**Find or list the rectangle dimensions and check the area.**
All three rectangles have area $16\text{ cm}^2$.

**Find the perimeters when needed.**
$P_{1\times16}=2\times(1+16)=34\text{ cm}$
$P_{2\times8}=2\times(2+8)=20\text{ cm}$
$P_{4\times4}=2\times(4+4)=16\text{ cm}$
Smallest to largest: $4\times4$, $2\times8$, $1\times16$.

**Compare the results or check the required condition.**
Smallest to largest: $4\times4$, $2\times8$, $1\times16$.

development.solution_text:

Find the missing width by dividing $48$ by $8$. Both areas are $48\text{ cm}^2$.

**Find the perimeters when needed.**
$w=48\div8=6\text{ cm}$
$P_{8\times6}=2\times(8+6)=28\text{ cm}$
$P_{12\times4}=2\times(12+4)=32\text{ cm}$
The $8\text{ cm}\times6\text{ cm}$ rectangle has the smaller perimeter by $4\text{ cm}$.

**Compare the results or check the required condition.**
$w=6\text{ cm}$; the $8\times6$ rectangle is smaller by $4\text{ cm}$.
